result:
"More agents always give better results" isn't true, so neither five nor ten is the right starting point.

Your budget makes this matter. Each extra agent re-reads shared context, sends coordination messages and summarizes results for handoffs. In Anthropic's testing, multi-agent setups typically used about 3–10x more tokens than a single agent on the same task. Teams also lost context at each handoff, and some got the same results from better prompting of one agent. Anthropic says multi-agent systems pay off mainly for high-value tasks with heavy parallel work, information too big for one context window, or very many complex tools ([source](https://claude.com/resources/articles/building-multi-agent-systems-when-and-how-to-use-them)).

Apply that to your assistant with a concrete request: "Can I use the laser cutter Thursday at 3?"

- The assistant looks up the manual, checks the calendar, then books. These steps are short and depend on each other.
- One agent with three tools can do all of it in one loop. Splitting it into a manual agent, a calendar agent and a booking agent would add handoffs and cost without adding capability.
- Some steps may not need an agent at all. For example, "after the calendar check succeeds, book the slot" can be a fixed workflow.

Splitting could pay off if you later find, say, that a manual-search subtask floods the context with long pages. A helper that returns only a short answer could then be worth its cost. Let evidence like that decide, not a target number.

My suggestion: start with one agent plus fixed workflow steps, measure cost per request, and split only where a measured problem justifies it. That is also an easy position to defend at your design review.

Quick check: in the Thursday-3pm request, which step would you make a fixed workflow rather than an agent decision, and why?

If you'd like, I can turn this into a lesson on workflows versus agents and when multi-agent pays off.

Sources:
- [Building multi-agent systems: When and how to use them](https://claude.com/resources/articles/building-multi-agent-systems-when-and-how-to-use-them)
